title: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the details of its construction.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But the phenomenon of universality implies that this is not the case, and that as soon as one has passed the threshold of universality, nothing more can in a sense ever be gained.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “The Rule 110 Cellular Automaton” (from p. 675), p. 675. Scope: all universal systems, of any type

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The saturation result is standard under extensional computability. Its informal 'nothing more' wording needs that qualification, but the intended context supplies it.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure capability as the class of partial computable functions realizable under effective encodings. Prove that every universal system realizes that same class and that no ordinary algorithmic rule realizes more.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The statement is false for resource efficiency, programmability, or physical capability unless capability is restricted to computability.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Within ordinary discrete models, universality means the ability to emulate a Turing machine, and any two such systems emulate each other. That theorem is textbook material and directly matches the claim that the set of computations stops growing once the threshold is passed. It does not say that more complicated rules are useless for speed or for ease of encoding.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Restrict capability to the set of input-output maps realizable with some encoding. Confirm if every Turing-universal system realizes exactly the partial recursive functions, so a more elaborate universal rule adds none; refute if some standard universal system computes a non-recursive function or if two universal systems realize different sets of maps.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Cost in time and space still depends on the rule, so a reading in terms of efficiency is not settled by extensional equivalence.

Intermediate Turing degrees show that not every non-simple system sits at this threshold; the claim concerns systems that have already passed it.
